blocks.text: Simple distillation separates the solvent from a solution. Take 100 cm3 of sea water and set up the apparatus (Figure 15.5), adding a few boiling chips to prevent bumping and making the apparatus air-tight so that no vapour escapes. Heat the flask gently with a Bunsen burner and let cold water circulate slowly around the condenser. Water (or alcohol) evaporates when its boiling point is reached, its vapour passes through the condenser, and the circulating water condenses it back to liquid: the distillate, collected in the receiving flask. The components left in the distillation flask are collectively the residue.

Separating two miscible liquids in this way is fractional distillation, successful only if the boiling points differ by about 25 degrees C. The distillation column, a glass column filled with glass beads to increase the surface area for condensing the vapour, separates the mixture into its components by boiling point (Figure 15.7). When a mixture of ethyl alcohol and water is heated, the alcohol distils first because its boiling point, 78 degrees C, is lower than water's 100 degrees C; while the alcohol distils the thermometer stays at 78 degrees C. As soon as the temperature starts to rise above 78 degrees C the receiving flask is replaced with a new one; when the thermometer reaches 100 degrees C water boils and is collected after condensation as the second distillate, so both components are obtained pure (Figure 15.6). Natural petroleum is a mixture of many compounds used as fuels, such as petrol, diesel, kerosene and furnace oil, whose boiling points are not very different; they are separated as fractions by fractional distillation in a fractionating column.

blocks.alt: Left: a distilling flask over a burner with a bead-packed fractionating column, a thermometer at the top, a sloping water-cooled condenser and a receiving flask, with labels. Top right: a graph of thermometer reading against time with a plateau at 78 degrees C while ethanol distils and a higher plateau at 100 degrees C while water distils. Bottom right: simple against fractional distillation and a glossary.
blocks.caption: Simple and fractional distillation apparatus and the ethanol-water temperature record (original diagram after Figures 15.6 and 15.7 and topics 15.3 and 15.2.1).
blocks.long_description: The liquid is boiled in a flask fitted with boiling chips, the vapour rises past a thermometer into a condenser cooled by running water, and the condensed distillate drips into a receiver while the non-volatile residue stays in the flask. For two miscible liquids a column packed with glass beads is added, giving many surfaces on which vapour condenses and re-boils, so that the lower-boiling liquid reaches the top first. With ethanol and water the thermometer holds at 78 degrees C while ethanol passes over, then climbs to 100 degrees C once only water is left, and the receiver is changed as the temperature begins to rise.
